findings.reason: The protected solution is concise, conventional, and interview-ready. The names trie, terminal, node, character, pairs, start, and end expose prefix storage, word completion, traversal state, output, and inclusive text boundaries directly. It has no exact generic local named index.

Inserting every word character by character creates exactly one trie path for each supplied word, with terminal marking every complete word even when it prefixes another. For each text start, the inner walk follows precisely the contiguous characters from that position and stops only when no supplied word can extend the current prefix. Reaching a terminal after consuming text[end] proves text[start:end + 1] is a word, and every occurring word necessarily follows its complete path and is reported. Restarting at every start preserves overlapping and nested matches. Starts increase globally and ends increase within each start, so emitted inclusive pairs already satisfy the required lexicographic order.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode problem 1065, Python, and the native indexPairs(text, words) interface. Authenticated source evidence confirms lowercase text of length 1 through 100, 1 through 20 unique lowercase words, and word lengths from 1 through 50. The app-local solve adapter preserves exact contiguous matching, inclusive [start, end] pairs, overlapping and nested occurrences, start-then-end ordering, empty-output behavior, and the list-of-pairs return contract.

The protected app source and immutable native source bound to verified submission 2067474630 are algorithmically identical: both build the same terminal-marked trie, traverse from every text start, advance through the same character edges, break on the same missing edge, append the same inclusive pair at every terminal node, and return pairs in traversal order. Their only structural differences are the required Solution.indexPairs wrapper and native typing syntax.

The three hidden workloads grow shared-prefix dictionaries from 5 through 20 words while text grows from 25 through 100 characters, a 4x span in both governing dimensions. Each unsuccessful word shares four leading characters, forcing a per-start/per-word matcher to repeat prefix work while the trie shares it. The exact protected source passed all eleven visible correctness cases and all three performance tiers with relative growth exponent -0.02 and a 1.02x largest runtime ratio. An independently correct cross-product matcher matched every correctness and benchmark output but failed only the calibrated complexity verdict at +0.67, distinguishing O(S+NL) trie traversal from O(NWL) direct matching.

The Approach accurately derives shared-prefix trie construction, terminal markers at multiple depths, traversal from every start, early stopping on a missing edge, and direct sorted output. It explicitly covers overlaps, nested words, no matches, and words longer than the remaining suffix. Its O(S+NL) time and O(S) auxiliary-space claims, excluding required output, match the protected implementation and branch manifest.

The modular Reference preserves exact contiguous word matching, inclusive pair bounds, start-then-end ordering, overlapping and nested occurrences, all five live constraints, both source examples in order, the second example's overlap explanation, and the source hint. The useful no-match case is now separately labeled under Additional Examples rather than represented as a third source example. The live statement contains no images, diagrams, tables, notes, or follow-up section.

The authenticated live Premium statement directly verified exactly two examples in source order with exact text, words, outputs, and only the second example marked with an overlap explanation; inclusive index pairs; lexicographic pair ordering; five constraints; and one independent-word-search hint. source_fidelity.json binds those facts and every composed local section to the reviewed statement hash 933f1273afd0ac8ba58b574f88d83b65237be9f7277957d6ac390ab317ef0832.

coverage: The authenticated Premium statement contains exactly two examples. Their exact inputs and ordered outputs appear first in source order; the former third sample is now correctly labeled as an additional no-match trial.

All eleven ordinary correctness cases are visible samples or trials. They cover text-length endpoints 1 and 100, word-count endpoints 1 and 20, word-length endpoints 1 and 50, lowercase input, and uniqueness across the maximum-size dictionary.

Material behavior includes inclusive endpoints, start-then-end ordering, overlapping occurrences, nested dictionary words, repeated matches at different positions, a whole-text word, shared prefixes, a word longer than the text, and empty output.

An independent oracle searches the text separately for every word, advances one position after each occurrence so overlaps are retained, converts matches to inclusive pairs, and sorts the final list. It recomputed every expected result without constructing or traversing a trie.

The oracle, protected app source, and immutable native Solution agreed on all 14 authored correctness-plus-benchmark inputs, 13230 exhaustive binary-alphabet text and non-empty dictionary combinations, 5000 deterministic random legal databases, and seven explicit boundary databases. The authored maximum boundary simultaneously exercises text length 100, 20 unique words, and word length 50.

The 5-, 10-, and 20-word workloads remain hidden and performance-only, use size consistently as word count while text length grows proportionally, and span 4x. A correct O(NWL) cross-product matcher matched every output and failed only scaling at +0.67, while the O(S+NL) protected trie passed at -0.02 and 1.02x.
